newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan opposition vows to fight for reforms.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan opposition vows to fight for reforms.

text.p: Kenyan opposition MPs said on Sunday they would organise more demonstrations if the government did not agree on constitutional reforms ahead of elections due later this year.

Their remarks followed six hours of running battles in the Kenyan capital Nairobi on Saturday between riot police and thousands of supporters intent on attending a rally on civil liberties. One man was killed and at least six were injured.
Police used teargas, batons, bayonets and live ammunition to disperse thousands of people who tried to gather in a field in a slum area in the east of the capital.
The crowd tried to enter the field known as Kamukunji, where many political demonstrations have been staged in the past years despite an order declaring the planned opposition rally illegal.
A coalition of opposition leaders and civil liberty advocates had called the rally to assert a constitutional right of free association.

James Orengo, vice-chairman of the Forum for Restoration of Democracy (FORD), told reporters on Sunday: "We are ready to go back to Kamukunji so long as constitutional reforms are not in place before the next general election."

Opposition parties say they are denied permits to hold meetings, and even when permits are granted their followers are sometimes arrested or harrassed. They want the lifting of some of the government's sweeping security powers.

A new party, Safina, has had no response to its application for registration submitted in 1995 -- four years after President Daniel arap Moi's Kanu party bowed to international pressure to end one-party politics and allowed opposition parties to run.
The Sunday Nation, Kenya's biggest-selling newspaper, warned that the continued frustration of opposition groups was spawning civil disobedience.
